item.title: ADB approves $300mn financing to ensure safe and resilient water services in Sri Lanka
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: To strengthen water sector governance, improve service delivery, enhance the resilience and promote greater private sect
item.content:encoded:
COLOMBO, SRI LANKA (9 November 2026) — The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved two projects totaling $300 million to expand and strengthen water supply and sanitation services across Sri Lanka.

“Access to safe, reliable, and sustainable water and sanitation services is essential for public health and economic growth,” said ADB Country Director for Sri Lanka Shannon Cowlin.

“These projects support the Government of Sri Lanka’s efforts to strengthen water sector governance, improve service delivery, enhance the resilience and financial sustainability of sector institutions, and promote greater private sector participation, helping ensure sustainable, and resilient water and sanitation services for Sri Lankans.”

The Climate-Resilient Sustainable Water Supply and Sanitation Project will provide $200 million to improve access to reliable and safe water supply services for more than 1.3 million people in the Western and Southern provinces, while improving sewerage and sanitation services for almost 250,000 people in Jaffna in the Northern Province.

The project will build new resilient water treatment plants, transmission and distribution networks, and storage reservoirs in Colombo and Lunugamwehera.

It will also develop wastewater treatment facilities, sewerage networks, and pumping stations in Jaffna.

The project will help reduce water losses, promote renewable energy use, strengthen the capacity of the National Water Supply and Drainage Board (NWSDB), and support private sector participation in the water sector.

The $100 million second subprogram of the Water Supply and Sanitation Reform Program—ADB’s first policy-based lending program in Sri Lanka’s water sector—builds on reforms introduced under the first subprogram.

It will strengthen water governance and service delivery and mobilize private sector financing for future investments.

The program supports reforms in two key areas.

First, it strengthens resilience, inclusion, and environmental sustainability through improved water resources management, water safety, sanitation management, and natural hazard adaptation.

Second, it strengthens governance and operational and financial performance through amendments to the National Water Resources Policy, tariff reforms, adoption of a resilience roadmap for the water supply and sanitation sector, stronger corporate performance management, implementation of NWSDB’s financial sustainability roadmap, and increased private sector participation.

It is aligned with Sri Lanka’s broader reform agenda to improve public services and promote green economic growth, while supporting the country’s commitment to address the impacts of natural hazards and extreme weather events.

Together, these investments and reforms will help deliver safer, more reliable, and more resilient water and sanitation services for communities across Sri Lanka.

item.title: Kelani Cables Sept quarter net profit up 4-pct to Rs634.5mn
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Financing performance, however, came under notable pressure from currency volatility.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lankan power and telecommunications cable manufacturer Kelani Cables PLC recorded a net profit of Rs. 634.53 million for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, rising 3.9 percent from Rs. 610.45 million in the same quarter last year, interim accounts showed.

The group posted basic earnings per share of Rs. 2.91 for the September quarter, up from Rs. 2.80 a year earlier, with prior period share counts and earnings adjusted to reflect a 1-for-10 share split executed in December 2025.

Quarterly group revenue expanded 19.4 percent to Rs. 6.43 billion from Rs. 5.38 billion, anchored by steady manufacturing throughput and resilient domestic cabling demand.

Cost of sales increased 20.3 percent to Rs. 5.21 billion from Rs. 4.33 billion, slightly outpacing top-line growth due to raw material input costs and production scaling. Despite this margin squeeze, gross profit rose 15.4 percent to Rs. 1.21 billion from Rs. 1.05 billion.

Operating overheads expanded as distribution costs climbed 13.0 percent to Rs. 233.91 million. Administrative expenses surged 37.0 percent to Rs. 178.70 million from Rs. 130.48 million, reflecting general inflationary adjustments and higher operating overheads. Operating profit nevertheless improved 12.2 percent to Rs. 805.55 million from Rs. 717.94 million.

Financing performance, however, came under notable pressure from currency volatility. While finance income grew 21.1 percent to Rs. 134.57 million, finance expenses spiked to Rs. 90.09 million against a credit of Rs. 27.09 million a year earlier. Notes to the financial statements revealed the group incurred a net foreign exchange loss of Rs. 63.18 million during the quarter, reversing sharply from an exchange gain of Rs. 26.22 million in the comparative period.

Consequently, net finance income fell 67.8 percent to Rs. 44.48 million from Rs. 138.22 million.

Share of profit from equity-accounted investee ACL-Kelani Magnet Wire (Pvt) Ltd turned around to Rs. 25,000, recovering from a loss of Rs. 164,000 previously.

Group pre-tax profit contracted marginally by 0.7 percent to Rs. 850.05 million from Rs. 855.99 million, weighed down by foreign exchange swings. However, a 12.2 percent decrease in income tax expense to Rs. 215.52 million helped cushion the bottom line, enabling net profit to finish higher.

Total group assets reached Rs. 19.98 billion as of September 30, 2026, with net asset value per share rising to Rs. 74.52 from Rs. 70.24 in March. Inventories increased to Rs. 5.14 billion from Rs. 4.19 billion, which drove short-term interest-bearing borrowings up to Rs. 786.87 million from Rs. 235.64 million to support working capital.

The company paid an interim dividend of Rs. 348.80 million during the first half.

Kelani Cables’ shares closed the September quarter at Rs. 98.60, having traded between a quarterly high of Rs. 108.50 and a low of Rs. 95.50. (Colombo/Nov09/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s WealthTrust Securities rebounds to profitability in 2Q 2026
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Amid volatile bond market conditions
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – WealthTrust Securities PLC, a licensed primary dealer in Sri Lanka, returned to profitability in the second quarter of the financial year 2026/27, recording a profit after tax of 154.6 million rupees for the quarter ended September 30, compared to a loss of 455.2 million rupees in the preceding quarter.

The recovery came amid continued volatility in the domestic government securities market, with the company maintaining its focus on prudent portfolio positioning and disciplined risk management.

“The return to quarterly profitability is encouraging, particularly in the face of continued volatility in the government securities market. Our focus remains on prudent risk management, maintaining a strong balance sheet and building a more sustainable and consistent earnings profile,” Romesh Gomez, Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of WealthTrust Securities PLC, said.

The quarter was characterised by significant movements in government securities yields.

Upward pressure on bond yields during July gave way to a strong rally through August, supported by favourable liquidity conditions, foreign investor demand, declining Treasury bill yields and limited new bond supply at auctions.

However, the momentum subsequently moderated, with renewed geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, elevated global oil prices and rising global bond yields contributing to a reversal in market sentiment towards the end of September.

Against this backdrop, the Company’s quarterly performance benefited from improved mark-to-market valuations, with net fair value gains of 170.8 million rupees, compared to net losses of 579.3 million rupees in the preceding quarter.

Net interest income remained a key contributor to earnings, amounting to 301.8 million rupees, while fee-based income and brokerage income contributed a further 27.0 million rupees and 1.4 million rupees, respectively.

Net realised capital losses of 241.3 million rupees continued to weigh on the quarterly result.

For the six months ended September 30, the company recorded a cumulative loss after tax of 300.7 million rupees, compared to a profit after tax of 437.1 million rupees in the corresponding period of the previous financial year.

Net interest income for the six-month period remained broadly stable at 667.1 million rupees, compared to 675.8 million rupees a year earlier.

However, combined net capital and fair value losses amounting to 787.1 million rupees, compared to net gains of 364.9 million rupees in the corresponding period of 2025, weighed on the overall half-year performance.

The company continued to maintain its regulatory ratios comfortably above the applicable minimum requirements, underpinned by a strong financial position, with net assets of 6.6 billion rupees and a total asset base of 50.6 billion rupees as at September 30.

WealthTrust Securities said it will continue to adopt a measured approach to market opportunities, with an emphasis on prudent portfolio positioning and disciplined risk management amid evolving market conditions. (Colombo/Nov9/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s Hambantota port, Al-Futtaim explore Gulf vehicle supply chain ties
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Discussions focused on expanding existing business relationships, the role of the CASCADIA RoRo Feeder Service,
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka’s Hambantota International Port Group (HIPG) and Al-Futtaim Logistics have held discussions to expand their commercial ties, as shipping disruptions in the Middle East position the southern port as a key vehicle transhipment gateway for Gulf markets.

The talks took place during a visit to the port by a delegation headed by the Vice Chairman of the UAE-based Al-Futtaim Group.

Discussions focused on expanding existing business relationships, the role of the CASCADIA RoRo Feeder Service, and potential investment opportunities across the port’s operations and industrial zone.

A white paper published by Al-Futtaim, titled Resilience in Motion, highlighted Hambantota as one of three alternative gateways deployed after supply routes were disrupted around the Strait of Hormuz in March 2026. The other two hubs were Port Sultan Qaboos in Muscat and Port Khor Fakkan in the Gulf of Oman.

Collectively, the three corridors moved over 25,000 finished vehicles into the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia.

“Alternative corridors brought into operation within weeks helped sustain dealer supplies and supported auto manufacturers in returning to full production capacity during the disruption,” An Al-Futtaim representative noted

Connectivity between Hambantota and onward vehicle supply chains in the Gulf has been bolstered by the CASCADIA RoRo Feeder Service, which was launched on June 9, 2026. The service is run by Canada-headquartered maritime specialist CASCADIA.

“Transhipment facilities located outside the immediate disruption zone provide practical alternative delivery routes that keep vital regional supply chains running smoothly,” the port operator said.

Talks also touched on broader contingency planning and regulatory coordination as global operators build resilient networks against future trade shocks. (Colombo/Nov08/2026)

item.title: Foreign investors exit Sri Lanka rupee bonds for third straight week
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Foreign investors have sold a net Rs. 28.5 billion worth rupee bonds in the last five weeks
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Foreign investors sold Sri Lanka rupee bonds and exited for a third straight week in the week ended on November 5, Central Bank data showed, despite slight appreciation in the rupee currency.

With the latest outflows, the island nation has seen net foreign selling in five of the last 21 weeks.

Offshore investors sold a net Rs. 6,075 million (US$218.4 million) worth of Sri Lanka rupee bonds in the week ended on November 5.

The net selling extended the net foreign outflows from the rupee bonds to Rs. 28.5 billion in the last five weeks.

Despite outflows in the last three weeks, the island nation has seen a total inflow of around Rs. 43.6 billion into local currency bonds so far this year, following a net inflow of 71.5 billion rupees last year.

Analysts said foreign investors sold rupee bonds in the week the U.S. mid-term election showed strong checks and balances for Trump’s presidential powers and hopes of an end to hostilities against Iran. It also came as the Israel Prime Minister failed to secure a majority in his election.

The rupee had been steady for more than three years before the sharp depreciation in May with the Central Bank citing higher oil and vehicle imports amid a lingering conflict in the Middle East.

The rupee has fallen 6.7 percent through November 6, this year.

Globally, investors are cautious about economic growth due to the impact of the latest Middle East escalation.

The rupee has stabilized after the Central Bank raised its key monetary policy rate by 100 basis points in May to curb inflationary pressure stemming from higher demand.

The island nation has seen an uptick in inflation in the last seven months following a nearly 50 percent hike in fuel prices.

The government raised fuel prices in the last week of October, raising further inflationary concerns.

Before the May rate hike, the Central Bank kept its key policy rates steady since May 2025 after reducing them by 825 basis points over 24 months since June 2023 and foreign investors have been buying rupee bonds. (Colombo/November 08/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s foreign reserves up 3.4-pct in Oct 2026; CB buys dollars
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Central Bank has bought net US$1.740 mln in first 10 months of 2026
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s foreign reserves gained 3.4 percent to US$ 7,086 million by the end of October 2026, up from US$6,851 million dollars a month earlier amid central bank purchasing US$191.3 million on a net basis in the month.

The Central Bank has been aggressively buying dollars to build up the reserves.

Analysts say the Central Bank’s year end reserve target of US$8 billion is achievable with the dollar inflows from the IMF and other multilateral institutions in the final quarter of 2026.

The Central Bank sold dollars in May amid sharp depreciation of the rupee currency that month.

The Bank sold over US$211 million net in May, marking the first net selling in 22 months.

The Central Bank has net bought US$1,740.1 million in the first 10 months of 2026 following a net purchase of US$2 billion last year.

The rupee was under high downward pressure in May as the imports bill for fuel rose unusually high following the Middle Eastern escalation amid continued demand for dollars to buy new vehicles.

However, it reversed course and gained in the next two months before falling in September and October.

The Central Bank has been buying dollars aggressively from the market to boost foreign currency reserves to meet the targets the country agreed with the IMF under the US$3 billion external fund facility and to repay the island nation’s multilateral and bilateral loans.

The Central Bank in May raised its Overnight Policy Rate amid heavy depreciation of the currency.

The Central Bank’s aggressive reserve building comes ahead of the repayment of foreign debts to sovereign bond holders. This repayment is scheduled to start from April 2028.

After successfully exiting sovereign default through a nearly-closed debt restructuring agreement and securing an IMF Extended Fund Facility (EFF) programme, Sri Lanka has been rebuilding its reserves to meet key targets for macroeconomic stability.

For debt repayment, adequate reserves are essential to meet upcoming external obligations without resorting to new borrowing or accumulating arrears.

While Sri Lanka has made significant progress in restructuring bilateral and commercial debts, any sustained erosion of reserves raises concerns about its ability to sustain the recovery trajectory and fully normalize relations with international markets.

Analysts say policymakers will likely need to focus on boosting export earnings, attracting foreign investment, and prudent fiscal management to reverse the decline and safeguard the hard-won gains from the IMF-supported programme. (Colombo/November 08/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka discussing private sector pension, housing benefits from EPF: Minister
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Sri Lanka’s largest single fund at over 6,000 billion rupees
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — The government is discussing plans to expand benefits from the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF), including a potential pension scheme, medical insurance, and housing projects for private sector workers, Minister of Trade, Commerce, Food Security and Cooperative Development Wasantha Samarasinghe said.

Speaking on the management of the fund, Samarasinghe said the administration aims to move beyond limiting EPF payouts strictly to retirement withdrawals.

“Even though the Employees’ Trust Fund is drawn every five years, the Employees’ Provident Fund can only be taken at age 50 for women and age 55 for men, once they retire. But this shouldn’t be limited merely to retirement,” Samarasinghe said.

The EPF, which operates alongside the 3 percent Employees’ Trust Fund (ETF), collects a 20 percent total contribution and stands as Sri Lanka’s largest single fund at over 6,000 billion rupees he said.

Samarasinghe noted that the fund had historically been treated merely as a source for state borrowing or subjected to mismanagement, stock market losses, and treasury bond controversies. He stressed that the present government, formed through the backing of the trade union movement, would safeguard its assets while delivering higher returns.

The discussions currently explore introducing a contributory pension model for private employees, modeled on the restoration of state pensions, as well as addressing sectors with low payouts such as the cooperative service, which employs over 20,000 workers.

“If a pension can be extended to private sector workers through a contributory pension model while safeguarding the assets of the Employees’ Provident Fund, we are actively engaged in discussions to secure that pension,” he said.

Samarasinghe told workers not to panic over changes to the fund’s management, adding that the state is acting with full understanding to protect employee rights. (Colombo/Nov07/2026)

item.title: Deloitte Sri Lanka brings together industry voices to examine Budget 2027
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: and its implications for business
item.content:encoded:
Sri Lanka’s transition from economic stabilisation towards sustainable growth is bringing reforms in fiscal policy, investment, trade and private-sector activity into sharper focus. Against this backdrop, Sri Lanka’s Budget 2027 will be a critical milestone for businesses seeking to understand the country’s evolving policy direction and what it could mean for investment, market positioning and future decision-making.

Pursuant to the 2027 Budget Speech presented in Parliament by the President, Deloitte Sri Lanka will bring together a distinguished panel of policymakers, economists, business leaders and industry representatives to examine the Budget’s key proposals and what they could mean for businesses and the wider economy.

The live webinar, “Beyond Stabilization: Building for Growth,” will be held under the theme “Explore Sri Lanka’s Budget 2027 and What It Means for You and Your Business.” Scheduled for Thursday, 12th November 2026, from 7.30 p.m. to 9.30 p.m. Sri Lanka time, the event will offer participants timely perspectives on the fiscal, economic, trade and industry priorities emerging from the Budget.

Designed to go beyond a conventional review of Budget announcements, the webinar will explore Budget 2027 through the interconnected perspectives of fiscal policy, economic outlook, trade and industry. By convening expertise from government, public policy, investment, think tanks and key industries, Deloitte Sri Lanka aims to provide participants with a broader understanding of the priorities, reforms and opportunities that could shape Sri Lanka’s next phase of growth.

The programme will feature two panel discussions, enabling participants to examine the Budget through distinct but complementary perspectives.

The first panel, “Fiscal Perspective,” will be moderated by Charmaine Tillekeratne, Partner and Head of Tax, Deloitte Sri Lanka and Maldives. The discussion will examine the country’s fiscal direction and significant Budget developments, connecting these measures with their broader relevance to businesses, investment and the economy.

Joining the discussion will be Hon. Chathuranga Abeysinghe, Deputy Minister of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development; Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya, Chief Advisor to the President of Sri Lanka on Digital Economy; Dr. Sulakshana Jayawardena, Director General of the Board of Investment of Sri Lanka; Dhananath Fernando, Chief Executive Officer of the ADVOCATA Institute; Yohan Lawrence, Secretary General of the Joint Apparel Association Forum; and Nihal Wijewardana, Senior Deputy Commissioner, Inland Revenue Department, Sri Lanka.

Drawing on perspectives from government, investment promotion and taxation, , the panel will offer participants an opportunity to consider Budget 2027 from multiple angles. The discussion will help connect national fiscal priorities with the operating realities, challenges and opportunities facing organisations across Sri Lanka.

The second panel, “Trade & Economy,” will be moderated by Ruvini Fernando, Head of Strategy, Risk & Transactions, Deloitte Sri Lanka and Maldives. It will broaden the conversation to Sri Lanka’s economic and trade landscape, examining the developments and priorities that could influence commerce, investment, infrastructure and industry.

The panel will feature Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma, Secretary to the Ministry of Finance; Dr. Indrajit Coomaraswamy, former Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka; Eng. Pubudu Niroshan, Member of the Power Sector Reforms Secretariat; Anushka Wijesinha, Co-Founder/Director of Centre for a Smart Future; Hemantha Gunetilleke, Chief Executive Officer of Nations Trust Bank PLC; and Zafir Hashim, President, Transportation Sector, John Keells Holdings PLC.

Together, the two discussions will create a platform where fiscal, economic, trade and industry perspectives converge. Deloitte Sri Lanka’s multidisciplinary approach is intended to help participants move beyond the immediate announcements and develop a clearer view of what the Budget could mean in practice for organisations navigating Sri Lanka’s changing economic environment.

Through “Beyond Stabilization: Building for Growth Budget Webinar,” Deloitte Sri Lanka aims to create a platform where fiscal, economic, trade and industry perspectives converge.

Business leaders, finance and tax professionals, investors and industry professionals are invited to join the conversation and explore what Budget 2027 could mean for their organisations and Sri Lanka’s economic direction.

Registrations are now open
Register for Deloitte Sri Lanka’s Budget 2027 webinar

item.title: Fitch affirms Sri Lanka’s Sierra Cables at ‘A+(lka)’; Outlook stable
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Reflects Sierra's Standalone Credit Profile (SCP) of 'a+(lka)', which is similar to that of its parent, LOLC Holdings PL
item.content:encoded:
Fitch Ratings – Singapore: Fitch Ratings has affirmed Sierra Cables PLC’s National Long-Term Rating at ‘A+(lka)’ with a Stable Outlook.

The National Long-Term Rating reflects Sierra’s Standalone Credit Profile (SCP) of ‘a+(lka)’, which is similar to that of its parent, LOLC Holdings PLC, in our view. The rating reflects our expectation of earnings growth, which are balanced against our forecasts for narrowing margins and rising leverage, alongside Sierra’s small operating scale and exposure to cyclical end markets and commodity price risk.

The rating also takes into account Sierra’s leading domestic position and growing export volumes. Limited liquidity headroom leaves Sierra reliant on lenders’ willingness to roll over working-capital facilities, while rising related-party transactions have further weakened its credit profile.

Key Rating Drivers
Domestic, Export Sales Boost Revenue: We expect Sierra’s leading position in the projects segment and cost advantage versus peers to support order wins and drive revenue growth. Sierra’s revenue rose 73% in the financial year ended 31st March 2026 (FY26) to LKR16.0 billion, driven by domestic and export sales growth.

Domestic sales growth is aided by Sierra’s efforts to strengthen its sales platform via dealer network expansion, promotions and a reinforced sales force. Revenue from tenders, Sierra’s highest-margin channel, fell in 4Q26 and 1Q27 due to Ceylon Electricity Board’s restructuring, but management expects activity to recover, with Sierra regaining momentum in recent bids.

Export Push Pressures Margins: Fitch expects export margins to remain thin, as Sierra prioritizes volume over pricing amid rising costs and competition. Export sales of about LKR5.0 billion in FY26 drove revenue growth. Shipments were mostly to the US. The company plans to invest about LKR2.0 billion to expand capacity dedicated to exports. Rising copper and aluminum prices add pressure on margins, while high competition from domestic rivals and imported cables curbs Sierra’s ability to pass through cost increases, limiting margin recovery.

High Working-Capital Intensity: Fitch expects the working-capital cycle to improve modestly but remain stretched at around 240 days over the next 12 months, versus 250 days in FY26. Sierra’s shift from cash to credit sales has increased working-capital intensity, with over 95% of sales now made on credit. Receivable days rose to 112 in FY26 from 64 in FY25, and Fitch expects these to be around 130-140 days over FY27-FY28. Inventory days have risen above 150 with recent sales growth, but should fall to about 130 days while payable days remain stable.

Debt-Funded Growth Lifts Leverage: Fitch expects leverage to remain high at close to 4.0x over the medium term as we expect the company to rely on debt to support growth. Sierra has funded its working capital and expansion capex mainly through debt over the last 24 months. The company has also raised funds via asset-backed securities to finance related-party receivables, mainly loans to LOLC. Leverage more than doubled over the last two financial periods, reaching 3.9x in FY26.

Government Spending Supports Growth: Fitch expects government development initiatives to drive growth in construction and renewable energy generation, benefiting Sierra through higher cable demand and a stronger operating environment. Sri Lanka’s economic recovery remains on track, with the government effectively absorbing shocks from Cyclone Ditwah and the Middle East conflict.

Rated on Standalone Basis: We assess Sierra on a standalone basis given our view that it is similar to that of the parent. However, Sierra’s rating is capped at one-notch above its parent’s consolidated credit profile if we assess the parent to be weaker than Sierra. This is based on our assessment of ‘Open’ ring-fencing and ‘Porous’ access and control by LOLC under our Parent and Subsidiary Linkage Rating Criteria.

Parent’s Credit Profile: Fitch’s assessment of LOLC reflects the conglomerate’s leading position in financial services, alongside interests in plantations, manufacturing, trading, real estate and leisure across 27 countries in Asia and Africa. LOLC generates most of its revenue from Sri Lanka. Fitch expects LOLC’s credit metrics to be stable in the near to medium term. EBITDA net leverage was high at about 10.0x in FY26, with EBITDA interest cover of 3.1x. Fitch de-consolidates LOLC’s finance, insurance and captive finance businesses under its criteria.

Peer Analysis
Sierra’s standalone rating is comparable with that of peers such as Singer (Sri Lanka) PLC (AA-(lka)/Stable), and Vidullanka PLC (A+(lka)/Stable).

Singer, one of the largest consumer durable retailers in Sri Lanka, has a wide branch and dealer network islandwide. Fitch rates Sierra one notch below Singer, reflecting Singer’s larger scale and stronger liquidity, which outweigh Sierra’s better leverage and interest coverage ratio (ICR). Singer’s leverage stands at 6.0x with ICR at 2.8x.

Vidullanka, a Sri Lankan renewable energy producer, is rated at the same level as Sierra, with a similar operational scale and EBITDA of about LKR2.3 billion. Vidullanka’s credit profile is stronger, with leverage around 2.1x and ICR above 6.0x. Sierra’s weaker credit profile is offset by lower counterparty risk, as its revenue is better diversified between private and government customers across products of varying specifications.

Fitch’s Key Rating-Case Assumptions
– Revenue to increase to around LKR19.6 billion in FY27 from LKR16.0 billion in FY26, driven by improved earnings from exports and the dealer network.

– EBITDA margin to decline to 19.1% in FY27 from 20.4% in FY26, due to higher raw material prices and thinner margins on export sales.

– Expansionary capex of LKR0.5 billion in FY27 to set up a new factory dedicated to exports, in addition to annual maintenance capex of LKR0.5 billion.

RATING SENSITIVITIES
Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Negative Rating Action/Downgrade:

– EBITDA net leverage over 4.0x for a sustained period.

– EBITDA interest coverage falling below 1.5x on a sustained basis.

– Weakening of Fitch’s assessment of LOLC’s credit profile together with revision of our assessment of LOLC’s ‘Access and Control’ over Sierra to ‘Open’, reflecting diminished minority shareholder influence and therefore a stronger effective control by LOLC over Sierra.

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Positive Rating Action/Upgrade:

– We do not expect any positive rating action in the near to medium term given the current largely debt funded expansion plans.

Liquidity and Debt Structure
Sierra reported cash and cash equivalents of LKR440.0 million at FYE26, compared with short-term debt maturities totaling LKR6.6 billion. The bulk of these short-term borrowings are used to fund working-capital requirements. Fitch expects Sierra to successfully roll over its short-term facilities and maintain liquidity at a manageable level.

Issuer Profile
Sierra is the third-largest cable manufacturer in Sri Lanka, with a broad range of products for several end-market uses.

REFERENCES FOR SUBSTANTIALLY MATERIAL SOURCE CITED AS KEY DRIVER OF RATING
The principal sources of information used in the analysis are described in the Applicable Criteria.

External Appeal Committee Outcomes
In accordance with Fitch’s policies the Issuer appealed and provided additional information to Fitch that resulted in a rating action that is different than the original rating committee outcome.

Report of Issuer’s Appeal
The issuer appealed the decision of the original rating committee.

In accordance with Fitch Ratings’ policies, the issuer’s request was reviewed by an appeal review panel, which determined that an appeal committee was warranted due to the availability of new information.

Relative to the original rating committee, the appeal committee updated Fitch’s assessment of the following Key Rating Drivers: Parent’s credit profile

The updates were of sufficient magnitude to affect the rating outcome.

The outcome of the appeal committee, as detailed within this rating action commentary, was different to the original rating committee outcome.

item.title: Sri Lanka stocks close up, ASPI up 0.52-pct

item.title: Sri Lanka rolls out ‘One TRADE’ single window portal for tea, coconut exports
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Serves as a single electronic entry point for traders to submit, receive, and process applications, declarations,
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka has launched a digital platform named “One TRADE” as the national single window for cross-border trade transactions, giving legal effect to electronic documentation across key export and import processes.

The One TRADE platform serves as a single electronic entry point for traders to submit, receive, and process applications, declarations, and data required by border authorities. Under the gazette, documents and communications processed through the portal are granted full legal validity.

The regulations were enacted under the Electronic Transactions Act through an extraordinary gazette issued on November 4. The rules took effect from November 5.

“These Regulations may be cited as the ‘Electronic Transactions (National Single Window for Trade) Regulations, No. 1 of 2026’,” the gazette stated.

GovTech Sri Lanka (Pvt) Ltd has been designated as the authorized operator of the system.

The initial rollout applies to the import, export, and transshipment of 124 tariff lines, with an immediate focus on Sri Lanka’s key agricultural exports including Ceylon tea, fresh and processed coconuts, copra, coir products, and arrack.

Participating border regulatory agencies include Sri Lanka Customs, the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, the Sri Lanka Tea Board, the Coconut Development Authority, the National Plant Quarantine Service under the Department of Agriculture, and the Food Control Administration Unit of the Ministry of Health and Mass Media.

Agencies are empowered to process, approve, or reject submissions directly via the digital channel within their existing legal powers. (Colombo/Nov06/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka poverty rises to 16-pct as inflation drives living costs up
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: "The substantial rise in the poverty line highlights the importance of accounting for changes in the cost of living
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s poverty headcount index rose to 16.0 percent in the first quarter of 2025 from 14.3 percent in 2019, reversing years of progress as high inflation drove up basic living costs, official survey data showed.

The Department of Census and Statistics Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2025 showed that 3.42 million people fell below the poverty line.

“The substantial rise in the poverty line highlights the importance of accounting for changes in the cost of living when assessing poverty trends.”

The official poverty line at the national level for September 2026 is 17,742 rupees.

The official poverty threshold jumped to 16,417 rupees per person per month in 2025 from 6,966 rupees in 2019.

The survey noted that the poverty headcount index had previously fallen steadily from 22.5 percent in 2012/13 to 16.0 percent in 2016 and 14.3 percent in 2019 before turning upward again amidst the 2022 economic crisis.

Across residential sectors, the estate sector recorded the highest poverty headcount index at 23.0 percent, with 205,624 people living in poverty.

The rural sector registered 17.3 percent poverty, accounting for the largest share with 2.93 million poor individuals.

The urban sector recorded the lowest poverty headcount index at 7.8 percent, representing 279,054 poor individuals.

“The poverty headcount ratio in Sri Lanka increased by 1.7 percentage points compared with 2019, suggesting a reversal of the previous declining trend.”

The DCS estimated the national poverty headcount index within a 95 percent confidence interval of 14.5 percent to 17.5 percent, with a coefficient of variation of 4.8 percent.

The survey, which covered a nationally representative sample of 25,000 housing units, was postponed from 2022 to 2025 due to exceptional economic conditions.

Finalized district-level data will be released later. (Colombo/Nov06/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka average household spend nears Rs116k a month in 2025
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The Department of Census and Statistics reported that nominal average monthly household expenditure surged 84.1 percent
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lankan household expenditure rose sharply to an average of 116,191 rupees per month in early 2025, driven largely by higher market prices, official data showed.

The Department of Census and Statistics reported that nominal average monthly household expenditure surged 84.1 percent from 63,130 rupees in 2019.

Median monthly household expenditure climbed from 47,544 rupees in 2019 to 94,057 rupees in 2025.

“The increase in average household expenditure was largely associated with rising prices, with only a modest increase in real expenditure over the period,” an official attached to the survey team said.

In real terms, adjusted for price changes using 2016 prices, average monthly household expenditure rose moderately to 63,734 rupees in 2025 from 55,430 rupees in 2019.

Real median monthly expenditure increased to 51,593 rupees from 41,745 rupees.

At the sector level, urban households spent the most, averaging 158,023 rupees per month, about 36 percent above the national average.

Rural households spent an average of 108,918 rupees, while estate households recorded the lowest monthly spending at 88,691 rupees.

“The findings highlight substantial differences across residential sectors, with urban households spending the most and estate households spending the least,” a statistical researcher commenting on the data said.

The preliminary findings were based on data collected across 25,000 households during the first quarter of 2025.

Average household size stood at 3.4 persons.

The DCS stated that the survey gathers consumption data across 35 subcategories — 19 food and 16 non-food groups. (Colombo/Nov06/2026)

item.title: Hemas Holdings Sept quarter net profit dips 3-pct to Rs2.0bn amid margin pressure, finance costs
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Top-line performance was led by the Hospitals sector
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka’s diversified conglomerate Hemas Holdings PLC recorded a net profit of Rs. 2.00 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, down 3.0 percent from Rs. 2.06 billion reported in the corresponding quarter last year, interim financial accounts showed.

The group posted basic earnings per share of Rs. 0.67 for the September quarter, down from Rs. 0.69 a year earlier.

Quarterly revenue rose 17.0 percent to Rs. 37.79 billion from Rs. 32.29 billion, driven by double-digit expansion across key segments.

Top-line performance was led by the Hospitals sector, which expanded 19.3 percent to Rs. 3.21 billion on higher medical admissions and increased channel consultations, while Consumer Brands jumped 18.3 percent to Rs. 15.57 billion.

Life Sciences, the largest revenue contributor, rose 16.2 percent to Rs. 18.37 billion, and Mobility grew 3.7 percent to Rs. 646 million.

The quarter also included the initial consolidation of East African learning solutions provider Twiga Stationers & Printers Limited in Kenya, following the acquisition of a 75 percent stake via Atlas Axillia on August 17, 2026, which added 1.40 billion rupees in provisional goodwill.

Cost of sales grew at a faster pace of 22.5 percent to Rs. 26.57 billion, restricting gross profit growth to 5.8 percent at Rs. 11.22 billion. Gross profit margin contracted by 3.1 percentage points to 29.7 percent.

Profitability was compressed as the group opted to absorb escalated input, energy, and logistics costs resulting from the Middle East conflict rather than passing the burden entirely onto consumers.

Price recovery was further constrained in regulated pharmaceuticals, where price revision mechanisms under the National Medicines Regulatory Authority (NMRA) faced ongoing delays.

Selling and distribution expenses fell 3.2 percent to Rs. 2.73 billion due to pruned direct marketing spend, while administrative expenses rose 12.6 percent to Rs. 4.95 billion, lifting operating profit by 8.1 percent to Rs. 3.78 billion.

However, finance costs surged 149.4 percent to Rs. 464.3 million as short-term bank borrowings and working capital lines increased to fund inventory build-ups ahead of the school season, extended distributor credit terms, and the Twiga acquisition. Net finance costs expanded to Rs. 248.7 million from Rs. 55.5 million.

Income tax expense rose 9.8 percent to Rs. 1.41 billion, leaving total group profit for the period down 1.7 percent at Rs. 2.12 billion.

Total assets reached Rs. 129.97 billion as of September 30, with net asset value per share rising to Rs. 19.22 from Rs. 17.06 a year earlier.

The board declared an interim dividend of Rs. 0.25 per share, payable on or before December 4, 2026.

Hemas Holdings’ shares closed at 31.00 rupees at the end of September and were trading around 30.90 to 31.20 rupees this week. (Colombo/Nov05/2026)

item.title: Cargills Ceylon Sept quarter net profit rises 9.4-pct to Rs3.0bn
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The group posted basic earnings per share of Rs. 11.80 for the September quarter
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka’s food and retail giant Cargills (Ceylon) PLC reported a net profit of Rs. 3.01 billion for the quarter ended September 30, rising 9.4 percent from Rs. 2.75 billion in the corresponding quarter last year, interim accounts showed.

The group posted basic earnings per share of Rs. 11.80 for the September quarter, up from Rs. 10.83 a year earlier.

Group revenue expanded 16.2 percent to Rs. 76.29 billion from Rs. 65.68 billion, driven by volume growth across all three core operational pillars: Retail, FMCG, and Restaurants.

Retail remained the group’s primary top-line contributor, generating Rs. 54.77 billion in net revenue, up 14.7 percent from Rs. 47.76 billion, anchored by a 13.2 percent same-store sales growth across Cargills Food City supermarkets. Growth was fueled by higher footfall alongside higher average basket sizes amid inflationary adjustments, with the network reaching 564 stores after opening 4 new outlets in Q2.

FMCG delivered the fastest top-line growth, surging 20.4 percent to Rs. 17.44 billion from Rs. 14.49 billion, underpinned by broad-based volume expansion across all key categories and selective price revisions to offset cost pressures. FMCG operating profit climbed 27.4 percent to Rs. 2.61 billion, supported by favorable product mix and ongoing cost optimization.

Restaurants brought in Rs. 4.07 billion in revenue, up 19.0 percent on 17.4 percent same-store sales growth, as KFC added 6 new outlets to reach 97 stores. However, restaurant operating profit slipped 4.0 percent to Rs. 685.4 million as management took a measured approach to menu price revisions to protect consumer affordability against steep operating cost increases.

Group cost of sales rose 16.2 percent to Rs. 66.40 billion, leaving gross profit up 15.9 percent at Rs. 9.89 billion.

Results from operating activities grew 13.6 percent to Rs. 5.59 billion. Operating profit growth was tempered by margin pressures as distribution expenses jumped 20.3 percent to Rs. 2.99 billion and administrative expenses rose 10.7 percent to Rs. 2.14 billion, reflecting higher energy, personnel, and logistics overheads.

Net finance costs expanded 22.3 percent to Rs. 1.16 billion from Rs. 948.5 million, pressured by higher interest expenses on increased short-term borrowings.

Profit before tax grew 11.4 percent to Rs. 4.47 billion, while income tax expenses rose 18.2 percent to Rs. 1.45 billion.

Total assets stood at Rs. 148.94 billion as of September 30, with net asset value per share increasing to Rs. 168.97 from Rs. 160.17 at the start of the financial year.

Cargills’ shares closed at 675.00 rupees at the end of September. Cargil’s share was at 645.75 rupees at the close of the day.  (Colombo/Nov05/2026)
